Placement is as claimed: in assert_select_only's walk loop (readonly.py:629-649) the exp.Select INTO check (637-638) comes first, then the exp.Lock check (643-645), then _refuse_denied_function (649). The consequence is not guaranteed. stmt.walk() is BFS by default (sqlglot core.py:1190-1196, bfs at 1209), so message precedence depends on node visit order, not only on line order. A denied function in the projection list (e.g. `SELECT sleep(1) FROM t FOR UPDATE`) is a sibling of the Lock node under Select. It is probably visited first, because expressions normally precede the lock arg, and would then report the denylist message instead of the locking-read message. A denied function nested in WHERE or a subquery sits deeper than the Lock node, so the lock message wins there. I did not run the parse to confirm the arg order. No test in the diff covers a statement holding both a denied function and a lock clause. Both cases are refused either way, and no requirement in the contract fixes which message wins. The command not run is sqlglot.parse_one('SELECT sleep(1) FROM t FOR UPDATE', read='mysql') followed by list(.walk()). No caller was found that depends on the old ordering: the redaction mapping in rule_sets.py keys on message text, and each message maps to a distinct redaction.

The claim is at docs/internal/database-connectors/read-only-safety.md:47. It matches the probe record in issue-context.md lines 14-16. That probe ran on a mysql:8.0 container (server 8.0.46) through PyMySQL with autocommit off, after SET SESSION TRANSACTION READ ONLY. FOR UPDATE, FOR UPDATE NOWAIT and FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED failed with (1792, 'Cannot execute statement in a READ ONLY transaction.'). FOR SHARE and LOCK IN SHARE MODE ran and returned rows. While the reading connection stayed open, a second session's UPDATE of a returned row failed with 1205 lock wait timeout. The same UPDATE succeeded right after the reading connection closed. This supports 'block other sessions' writes until the connection closes'. Absolute-claim input: a commit or rollback would release the locks earlier. With autocommit off and one connection per run_sql call, closed in finally (issue-context.md line 54), nothing commits before the close, so the probe's close-based release holds. I traced this through the issue's probe record only. I did not re-run MySQL.
